cards.definition: A central character whose fatal flaw leads to their downfall. Romeo's impulsiveness and Juliet's defiance both contribute to the tragedy.
A central theme exploring whether the lovers are doomed by destiny ('star-crossed') or destroyed by the choices of those around them.
The opening sonnet that reveals the tragic ending in advance, creating dramatic irony throughout the play.
When the audience knows something a character does not, e.g. the audience knows Juliet is alive when Romeo believes she is dead.
A social structure where men hold authority. Capulet's control over Juliet's marriage reflects the rigid gender expectations of the era.
An idealised, worshipping form of love seen in Romeo's infatuation with Rosaline, contrasting with his deeper love for Juliet.
A key male value — Tybalt and Mercutio's deaths stem from conflicts rooted in the need to protect personal and family honour.
Present on multiple levels: family (Capulet vs Montague), internal (Romeo's loyalty vs love), and social (individual desire vs expectation).
Used repeatedly to reflect contradiction, e.g. 'O brawling love, O loving hate' — showing the paradox of the lovers' situation.
14-line poems in iambic pentameter used for the prologue and the lovers' first meeting, elevating their relationship as pure and poetic.
Romeo's witty, cynical friend who dismisses romantic love. His death at Tybalt's hands is the turning point that seals the tragedy.
Juliet's aggressive cousin who embodies the feud. His refusal to compromise drives the play towards tragedy.
A well-intentioned but flawed figure whose plan to reunite the lovers ultimately fails, raising questions about adult responsibility.
Juliet's confidante and maternal figure. Her later advice to marry Paris represents a pragmatic but devastating betrayal of Juliet.
Juliet's father whose initial reasonableness turns to aggressive control when she refuses to marry Paris, showing the dangers of patriarchal power.
Juliet is Romeo's 'sun', yet their love exists in darkness and secrecy, suggesting its fragility and the danger surrounding it.
A key theme — the speed of the lovers' relationship, marriage and deaths reflects passion, but also causes their destruction.
Death is personified as Juliet's bridegroom, e.g. 'Death is my son-in-law'. This motif foreshadows and contextualises the tragic ending.
The Prince, the families and the Friar all bear responsibility for the tragedy. Shakespeare critiques a society that values honour over human life.
A rhythm of ten syllables per line. Higher-status characters often speak in it; prose is used for lower-status or comic moments.
The central theme — Scrooge's transformation from a cold, miserly man to a generous one shows Dickens's belief that anyone can change.
Dickens's key message — the wealthy have a moral duty to help the poor. Scrooge's neglect of this duty is presented as both wrong and dangerous.
Two allegorical children beneath the Ghost of Christmas Present's robes, representing the suffering caused by society's wilful neglect of the poor.
The novella works as an allegory — characters, settings and events symbolise wider moral and social truths about Victorian England.
Scrooge's dead business partner who appears in chains — the physical symbol of the spiritual punishment awaiting those who ignore their fellow human beings.
Represents memory and regret. Shows Scrooge's lonely childhood and lost love, helping the reader understand why he became cold and isolated.
A jolly, generous figure who shows Scrooge the warmth of others' celebrations including the Cratchits, highlighting what Scrooge has chosen to reject.

cards.keyword: The Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come
cards.definition: A silent, shadowy figure representing death and consequence. Shows Scrooge his lonely, unmourned death if he does not change.
Bob Cratchit's disabled son who symbolises the innocent poor. His potential death is used to shock Scrooge and the reader into empathy.
Dickens wrote the novella in 1843 in response to a report on child poverty, using fiction to campaign for social reform.
Scrooge moves through fear, regret and empathy across the five staves, ending as a man who embraces generosity and community.
Scrooge's underpaid clerk who represents the decent, hardworking poor. His warmth despite poverty contrasts sharply with Scrooge's wealth and coldness.
Scrooge's cheerful nephew whose repeated invitation to Christmas dinner symbolises forgiveness and the warmth that Scrooge has been shutting out.
Dickens calls each chapter a 'stave' (part of a musical score), reinforcing the carol theme and suggesting the novella is a joyful moral fable.
Darkness represents Scrooge's isolation and moral blindness; light represents generosity and redemption. The novella ends with brightness.
Christmas represents generosity, community and compassion — a time that exposes the moral state of individuals.
Scrooge's kind former employer who shows that wealth and generosity are not mutually exclusive, implicitly criticising Scrooge's choices.
Scrooge's former fiancee who leaves him because he replaced love with money, representing what Scrooge has sacrificed.
Dickens uses vivid comparisons to establish Scrooge — 'Hard and sharp as flint' — making his character instantly clear to the reader.
Dickens uses a warm, intimate narrator who addresses the reader directly, creating a moralistic tone that reinforces the novella's message.
Priestley's central message — we are all responsible for each other. Each Birling family member's selfishness contributed to Eva Smith's death.
A mysterious figure who may represent conscience or socialist ideals. His name ('ghoul') and omniscience suggest he is more than a real detective.
The unseen victim whose death drives the plot. She may be one woman or many — symbolising all exploited working-class women.
A pompous businessman who prioritises profit over people. Priestley uses him to satirise capitalist values and wilful ignorance.
Arthur's cold, snobbish wife who refuses to accept responsibility. Her dismissal of Eva's charity appeal is presented as especially callous.
Initially shallow, she undergoes the greatest change — accepting responsibility and emerging as a moral voice representing hope for a better future.
The troubled son whose theft and relationship with Eva reveals his weakness and the hypocrisy of the Birlings' respectability.
Sheila's fiance whose affair with Daisy Renton reveals his capacity for both kindness and exploitation. His relief at the Inspector's exposure is telling.
Set in 1912 but written in 1945. The dramatic irony of Birling's wrong predictions about war and the Titanic undermines his authority.
Sheila and Eric accept responsibility; Arthur and Sybil do not. Priestley suggests hope lies with the younger generation.
The audience knows Birling is wrong about war and the Titanic, making his dismissal of social responsibility seem even more arrogant.
No single character kills Eva — each plays a part. Priestley argues that society's collective indifference causes suffering.
The Birlings' treatment of Eva is shaped by class prejudice. Priestley exposes how the privileged exploit the vulnerable with impunity.
Eva is vulnerable partly because she is a woman — she can be dismissed from work, manipulated by men and turned away from charity.
'We are members of one body. We are responsible for each other.' This directly states Priestley's socialist message to the audience.
The final phone call resets the plot, suggesting the cycle of suffering will continue unless attitudes change — a warning to the 1945 audience.
One location, one evening. This creates intensity and claustrophobia, trapping characters with their guilt.
Birling represents capitalism (individual profit); the Inspector represents socialism (collective responsibility). Priestley clearly sides with the Inspector.
Written at the end of WWII, the play argues that post-war Britain must choose a fairer, more equal society — or repeat the mistakes of the past.
The Inspector may represent conscience or moral reckoning. His supernatural qualities suggest the Birlings cannot ultimately escape responsibility.
A sonnet about a ruined statue in the desert. Explores the idea that political power is temporary and nature/time will always outlast human arrogance.
A walk through London exposing suffering and oppression. Blake criticises the institutions — church, monarchy, government — that maintain poverty.
Explores how nature disciplines and humbles the speaker. A terrifying experience on a lake reveals nature's power over human arrogance.
A dramatic monologue in which a duke reveals he had his wife killed for not deferring to him. Explores controlling, possessive power.

cards.keyword: The Charge of the Light Brigade (Tennyson)
cards.definition: Celebrates soldiers ordered into a suicidal cavalry charge. Explores the tension between military glory and the catastrophic waste of war.
Soldiers dying from cold and boredom rather than battle. Challenges the idea that war is glorious — nature is the real enemy here.
Explores a community's vulnerability to nature's power. The storm becomes a metaphor for any overwhelming, invisible force — including political conflict.
A soldier's chaotic, terrifying experience mid-charge. Hughes strips away patriotism to expose the animal fear and confusion of combat.
A soldier haunted by shooting a looter. Explores psychological trauma (PTSD) and the lasting damage of conflict on those who fight.
A mother's grief as her son leaves for war. Explores the domestic, personal cost of conflict — the power of love and loss.
Explores the moral tension of documenting suffering. The photographer feels guilt and detachment — the public's indifference is also critiqued.
Uses paper as a metaphor to explore the fragility of human power and the structures we build — maps, records, religious texts — to control our lives.
A speaker remembers a city she was forced to leave. Explores the power of memory and identity against political oppression.
A Japanese pilot turns back from a suicide mission. Explores the conflict between duty and the will to live — and the community's punishment of his choice.
Challenges a colonial education that erased Black history. Uses dialect and fragmented form to reclaim cultural identity and resist oppression.
A poem spoken by a single voice, often revealing character unconsciously. Used in My Last Duchess and Remains to expose uncomfortable truths.
A turn or shift in argument or tone within a poem — often the moment a key idea is challenged, complicated or extended.
When a sentence continues beyond the end of a line without a pause. Can create momentum, breathlessness or a sense of being out of control.
Several poems use nature to represent an overwhelming force that exposes the limits of human power — Wordsworth, Heaney and Owen all explore this.
How poets arrange stanzas, lines and punctuation to create meaning. Regular form can suggest control; fragmented form can suggest chaos or oppression.
